title: Phishing & Social Engineering Security Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect against phishing scams and social engineering attacks. Learn to spot fake emails, verify legitimacy, and stay secure.
intro: Phishing attacks and social engineering scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated, using AI and brand impersonation to trick even cautious users. This comprehensive checklist helps you identify threats, verify legitimacy, and protect yourself from cybercriminals targeting your personal information and finances.

items.why: Scammers often use lookalike domains or spoofed addresses that appear legitimate at first glance but contain subtle misspellings.
items.howTo: Hover over the sender's name to see the full email address. Look for typos, extra characters, or domains that mimic real companies (like 'arnazon.com' instead of 'amazon.com'). When in doubt, contact the company directly through their official website.

items.task: Look for urgent language and suspicious requests
items.why: Phishing emails create false urgency to pressure you into acting quickly without thinking, often requesting sensitive information legitimate companies wouldn't ask for via email.
items.howTo: Be suspicious of phrases like 'urgent action required,' 'verify account immediately,' or 'limited time offer.' Legitimate companies rarely ask for passwords, Social Security numbers, or credit card details via email.

items.why: Malicious links can lead to fake websites designed to steal your credentials or download malware onto your device.
items.howTo: Hover over links to see the destination URL in your browser's status bar. Look for suspicious domains, URL shorteners, or addresses that don't match the claimed sender. Use a privacy-focused browser's enhanced security features when visiting unfamiliar sites.

items.why: Email attachments are common vehicles for malware, ransomware, and viruses that can compromise your entire system.
items.howTo: Never open unexpected attachments, especially.exe,.zip, or.pdf files from unknown senders. Use antivirus software to scan all attachments. When possible, ask senders to share files through secure cloud services instead.

items.why: While scammers are getting better at copying legitimate company designs, they often miss subtle details or use lower-quality graphics.
items.howTo: Compare suspicious emails with legitimate ones from the same company. Look for pixelated logos, inconsistent fonts, poor grammar, or layout issues. Legitimate companies maintain consistent professional branding standards.

items.why: The most reliable way to verify suspicious communications is to contact the organization directly through methods you know are legitimate.
items.howTo: Instead of using contact information from the suspicious email, visit the company's official website or call their published phone number. Ask if they sent the communication in question.

items.why: Social engineers use publicly available personal information to make their attacks more convincing and personalized.
items.howTo: Review privacy settings on social media platforms. Limit who can see your posts, contact information, and personal details. Avoid sharing vacation plans, work details, or family information publicly.

items.task: Question unsolicited phone calls requesting information
items.why: Phone-based social engineering attacks often impersonate trusted organizations to extract sensitive information or convince victims to take harmful actions.
items.howTo: Never provide personal information, passwords, or financial details over unsolicited phone calls. Ask for the caller's name and department, then hang up and call the organization's official number to verify.

items.task: Authenticate IT support and technical assistance requests
items.why: Fake technical support scams are extremely common, often targeting less tech-savvy users with claims of computer infections or security issues.
items.howTo: Legitimate IT support will never cold-call you about computer problems. If someone claims to be from Microsoft, Apple, or your ISP offering help, hang up and contact them directly. Never allow remote access to your computer from unsolicited contacts.

items.task: Verify claims of authority or urgency
items.why: Social engineers often impersonate authority figures or create fake emergencies to bypass your normal skepticism and security practices.
items.howTo: When someone claims to be from law enforcement, government agencies, or company executives demanding immediate action, take time to verify independently. Real emergencies allow time for proper verification.

items.why: Pretexting involves creating fake scenarios to build trust and extract information, often appearing as market research, surveys, or friendly conversation.
items.howTo: Be cautious of unsolicited surveys asking for personal information, 'verification' calls from services you use, or friendly strangers asking detailed questions about your work, family, or habits.

items.why: Spear phishing uses personal information to create highly convincing, targeted attacks that are much harder to detect than generic phishing attempts.
items.howTo: Be extra suspicious of emails that reference specific personal details, recent purchases, or current events in your life. Even if the email seems personalized and legitimate, verify through independent channels before acting.

items.why: Artificial intelligence now enables scammers to create more convincing emails, fake websites, and even voice calls that are harder to distinguish from legitimate communications.
items.howTo: Look for subtle inconsistencies in tone, context, or details that don't quite match previous communications from the same source. When in doubt, verify through multiple channels before trusting any request.

items.why: Email security tools can automatically detect and filter many phishing attempts before they reach your inbox, providing an additional layer of protection.
items.howTo: Consider using email clients with built-in phishing protection, browser extensions that check links, or dedicated anti-phishing software. Enable spam filters and phishing warnings in your email client.

items.task: Enable two-factor authentication on all accounts
items.why: Even if phishing attacks successfully steal your password, two-factor authentication provides a crucial second barrier against account compromise.
items.howTo: Enable 2FA on email accounts, financial services, social media, and any service that handles sensitive information. Use authenticator apps rather than SMS when possible for better security.

items.task: Regularly monitor accounts for suspicious activity
items.why: Early detection of compromise allows you to respond quickly and minimize damage from successful attacks.
items.howTo: Check bank statements, credit reports, and account activity regularly. Set up account alerts for logins, purchases, and changes. Report suspicious activity immediately to the relevant institutions.

items.task: Maintain updated security software and browsers
items.why: Updated software includes the latest security patches and phishing detection capabilities to protect against new threats.
items.howTo: Enable automatic updates for your operating system, browsers, and antivirus software. Consider using security-focused browsers like a privacy-focused browser that provide enhanced protection against malicious websites.

pro_tips: Trust your instincts - if something feels suspicious, it probably is. Take time to verify rather than acting immediately on urgent requests.
Use a password manager to avoid manually entering credentials on potentially fake websites - legitimate sites will auto-fill, fake ones won't.
Keep a 'verification contact list' with official phone numbers and websites for important services, so you always have trusted ways to confirm suspicious communications.
Practice the 'pause principle' - legitimate organizations will never pressure you to act immediately without allowing time for verification and consideration.
Report phishing attempts to help protect others - forward suspicious emails to the Anti-Phishing Working Group at reportphishing@apwg.org and report to the relevant companies being impersonated.
